title: Sample Scenes and Order
concept: Test game: read the move in a scene, keep the meters up, and put the steps of a clean apology in order.
bookIdea: A game is a set of covert moves that end in a bad feeling, and it can be spotted from the moves alone.

opener.setting: Tuesday, 6:40pm. The school gate, Kothrud, the cold part of the evening.

lines.text: “You didn't ring me back on Sunday. Again.”
“I know. I said I would. Things got in the way.”

opener.ask: In each scene, which line keeps the meters up, and which line starts a game?

items.text: “You didn't ring me back on Sunday. Again.”
items.why: Aai names a missed call and a repeat. She is giving Rohan a clear sting, which is a negative stroke for a repeated slip.

traps.1: Trade would be a proposal with a request and an answer built in. Aai has not offered anything yet, so this is a complaint, not a deal.

items.example:
Family group chat: “You forgot the bins again.”
That is one small sting, and it is about the bins, not about a deal.

items.text: “I know. I said I would. Things got in the way.”
items.why: The line is a small, sorry apology said to the pavement. It sounds like a child caught out, not like a parent or a grown-up with a plan.

traps.0: Parent would sound like “You should know better than to miss a call.” It sets a rule about the other person's habits.
traps.1: Adult would give a plan: “I'll ring you tonight at eight.” It names a time, which this line does not.

items.example:
A teacher at parents' evening: “You know the rules, so please be on time.”
That is the Parent voice, handing down a rule.

items.text: “So what do you want me to do with that, then?”
items.prompt: What is the move in this line?
items.why: The line opens a fight the other person is meant to answer, with the same tone pushing back. That pattern marks it as the start of a game.

traps.0: Ritual would be the same question asked at the same time every week, with a set answer that both people know by heart.

items.example:
At a bus stop: “So you're going to be late again, then?”
The question is a hook, and the answer is what the hook is for.

rounds.label: Play, the week in motion
rounds.intro: Each scene runs a few beats. Pick a line at each beat and watch the meters.

items.title: Tuesday, 6:40pm, the school gate
items.setting: Aai is cold and Rohan is late. The two of them need to agree on the call.

beats.text: “Sorry, sorry, I owe you for the call. Again.”

lines.outcome: Aai takes the out, and the call never gets scheduled.
lines.why: A quick pardon keeps the peace for a minute but keeps the old loop running.

lines.text: “You owe me for the call and the last two weeks. Ring me Friday.”
lines.outcome: Aai goes quiet, then nods and says Friday.
lines.why: A clear, specific ask keeps the exchange honest and gives the other person a way to pay.

beats.text: “Can we not do this before work?”

lines.outcome: Rohan leaves on time, and the subject waits until Friday.
lines.why: Naming a time for the talk keeps both of you honest.

lines.text: “Right. This is the last time I cover for you. Done.”
lines.outcome: Rohan stops with the car door open and says nothing for a while.
lines.why: The line seems to end the matter, but it sets up a point to win. It is a game move, so the scene stops here.

lines.text: “Okay. Then tell me what you need from me this week.”
lines.outcome: Rohan softens and names two things he can do.
lines.why: A question that asks for information is fair, though it is not the cleanest move.

beats.text: “So, Friday? You'll tell me the number?”

lines.text: “Friday. Write it on the fridge so we both see it.”
lines.outcome: Aai laughs and writes it on the fridge.
lines.why: A written note turns a promise into a shared fact.

lines.outcome: The promise drifts, and the number is never said.
lines.why: A vague yes gives the other person nothing to check on.

items.payoff: Aai takes the silence as a yes. The call stays unpaid, and the same argument starts again on Friday.

fallout.them: Rohan is already in the car, and the scene has nothing left to say.
fallout.you: You have run out of things to say, so the scene stops here.

items.title: Tuesday, 6:55pm, the same gate
items.setting: A second try at the same call. The gate is emptying.

beats.text: “You didn't ring me back on Sunday. Again.”

lines.text: “I'm sorry. I'll ring you tonight at eight, and I mean it.”
lines.outcome: Aai nods, a little less stiff.
lines.why: An apology that names a time gives the other person something to check.

lines.outcome: Aai says nothing and turns to the gate.
lines.why: A short brush-off is not cruel, but it spends the other person's patience.

beats.text: “So what do you want me to do with that, then?”

lines.text: “Tell me what you need from me, and I'll try to do it.”
lines.outcome: Aai softens and starts listing things.
lines.why: An open question hands the next move back to the other person.

lines.outcome: The gate door opens and Aai walks in without a word.
lines.why: Withdrawing ends the scene quietly, and it costs both of you.

lines.text: “Eight o'clock. I'll be on the balcony.”
lines.outcome: Aai waves over her shoulder and says, see you then.
lines.why: A place and a time turn a promise into a plan.

lines.outcome: Aai leaves, and the call is still only a word.
lines.why: A flat yes is fine, but it leaves nothing to check.

fallout.them: Aai has gone in, and the call at eight will not happen.

items.prompt: Put these steps of a clean apology in order.

items.text: “I was late, and I didn't tell you.”
items.why: Name what happened first, with no excuse in front of it.

items.text: “That left you waiting at the gate for twenty minutes.”
items.why: Then say what it cost the other person, in plain words.

items.text: “Next time I'll message you from the bus.”
items.why: Name a specific fix that the speaker can actually do.
End by asking, so the other person can answer and the matter can close.

items.example: Team stand-up: “I missed the nine o'clock call. I'll message the group from now on. Does that work for you?”

debrief.meera: One move at a time is how these scenes run. Aai's question was the hook to watch: a plain answer keeps the meters up, and a withdrawal costs both of you. The steps of a clean apology are short, and the last one is a question you can answer.
debrief.bookNote: The books call this a game, a set of covert moves that ends in a bad feeling for everyone at the table.

reflection.prompt: Think of a time this week when a small apology stopped a fight, or started one. What was the second line?
